Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Tracing and Line of Sight
Tracing and Line of Sight
Cast rays and swept shapes from C++ to detect, highlight, and interact with actors.
In this lesson

You will learn line traces, shape traces, reading FHitResult, configuring collision channels and query params, plus debugging and performance recommendations for reliable interactions.

Why it matters

Tracing is the backbone of look-based interaction, hitscan weapons, and spatial queries. Correct setup prevents false hits and costly frame spikes.

screens.title: What is Tracing (Raycasting)?
screens.narratorSegment: Tracing, also called raycasting, is the act of sending an invisible probe into the game world to check what it intersects. At its simplest, a line trace defines a start point and an end point; the engine walks that straight path and reports any collisions. In Unreal Engine C++ this returns an FHitResult containing the actor and component hit, the hit location, the surface normal, and other details like bone name for skeletal meshes. Think of a flashlight beam: where the beam meets an object you can learn what that object is and how to respond. A common gameplay example is pointing at a pickup item — a trace from the camera detects the item so you can show a UI prompt or pick it up. A misconception to avoid is assuming the trace always hits something. You must check the hit flag before reading fields, otherwise you risk null access. Another misconception is that traces are always cheap; they can become expensive if you run complex multi-shape traces every frame across many actors. The core takeaway is that tracing is a precise way to query the world, but you must control what you query and how often. How might you use tracing to determine whether an NPC is visible from the player’s vantage?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Tracing casts a ray or swept shape to detect collisions and returns an FHitResult with detailed hit information.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › What is Tracing
Definition

A trace checks a path or swept shape for collisions and returns an FHitResult with actor, component, location, normal, and optional bone name for skeletal hits.

Analogy
Imagine a flashlight beam: whatever the beam meets is what the trace reports. Use it to let the player look at and interact with objects.
Common misconception
Never assume a hit. Always check FHitResult.bBlockingHit or IsValidBlockingHit before using result fields.
Concrete Example
A player looks at an item. The game casts a line from the camera forward. If the trace hits a static mesh that blocks Visibility, the item highlights so the player can press interact.
Key Takeaway

Tracing is the canonical way to determine what is in a path or volume; use it deliberately and check results before using them.

screens.title: Line Trace Walkthrough in C++
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a basic line trace pattern you will use frequently. The necessary inputs are a start location, an end location — usually start plus a forward vector times distance — and a collision channel to query, such as Visibility. In C++, you prepare an FHitResult and an FCollisionQueryParams object. Important query settings include adding the actor performing the trace to the ignore list and setting bTraceComplex if you need per-polygon accuracy. Call LineTraceSingleByChannel on UWorld and check its boolean return. If true, read HitResult. GetActor(), HitResult. Location, and HitResult. Normal. A concrete example is tracing 200 or 500 units forward from the camera to detect interactable props. A common mistake is forgetting to ignore the owner; the trace may immediately hit the performing actor and return itself. Another nuance is the difference between simple collision and complex collision: simple is faster and usually sufficient for gameplay highlighting, while complex enables bone-level accuracy when you need exact hit points on a skeletal mesh. As a quick check, draw a debug line colored green on hit and red on miss so you can see the behavior while testing. How will you decide trace distance in your project?

keyIdea.title: Pattern
keyIdea.text: Set start/end, configure query params, call LineTraceSingleByChannel, check return and FHitResult before using hit data.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Line Trace Walkthrough
Starter Code Example
#include "Kismet/KismetSystemLibrary.h"
#include "DrawDebugHelpers.h"

FVector Start = GetPawnViewLocation();
FVector End = Start + GetPawnViewRotation().Vector() * 500.0f;
FHitResult Hit;
FCollisionQueryParams Params;
Params.AddIgnoredActor(this);
Params.bTraceComplex = false;

bool bHit = GetWorld()->LineTraceSingleByChannel(
  Hit, Start, End, ECC_Visibility, Params
);

if (bHit && Hit.GetActor()) {
  // Use Hit.GetActor(), Hit.Location, Hit.Normal
}
The example uses Visibility as the channel and ignores the tracing actor to avoid self-hits.
Explanation & Example
  • Start is often the camera location; end is forward vector times range.
  • Check the function boolean then use Hit to get actor and hit details.
  • Visualize with DrawDebugLine to confirm orientation and hit status.
Key Takeaway

Define start/end and query params reliably and never dereference hit fields without checking the result.

screens.title: Understanding FHitResult
screens.narratorSegment: FHitResult is the structured response you get after a trace and is central to deciding how to react. The most used fields are GetActor or HitActor, which tells you the actor hit; HitComponent gives the specific primitive component; Location is the world position of the impact; Normal describes the surface orientation at the hit point; and BoneName is available when hitting a skeletal mesh. A practical example: when detecting a headshot you rely on BoneName to confirm the limb hit, but only after you used complex collision to get per-polygon detail. Another vital aspect is the hit validity flags. Use bBlockingHit or IsValidBlockingHit to guard access. Beginners often try to cast the actor right away and crash because the trace returned no hit. Also beware that Location and Normal are only meaningful when a hit occurred; they may be zero or undefined otherwise. As a check during development, log or display the values you read from FHitResult to ensure they match expected geometry. The core takeaway is: read FHitResult carefully, guard access, and use the right collision complexity to get the fields you need.

keyIdea.title: FHitResult
keyIdea.text: Contains actor, component, hit location, surface normal, and optional bone name; always check hit validity flags before use.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Understanding FHitResult
Key Fields
  • GetActor / HitActor: The actor that was hit.
  • HitComponent: The primitive component impacted.
  • Location: World position of the impact.
  • Normal: Surface normal at the hit point.
  • BoneName: For skeletal meshes when complex collision is used.
Practical Guidance
Always check bBlockingHit or IsValidBlockingHit before using fields. When you need limb-level detail use bTraceComplex true so BoneName becomes reliable. Use these fields to decide interactions, play effects at hit location, or orient decals with the normal.
Example
On hit, spawn an impact decal at HitResult.Location aligned to HitResult.Normal to visually communicate the collision.

screens.title: Collision Channels and Object Types
screens.narratorSegment: Collision channels and object types determine what a trace actually hits. Unreal provides built-in channels like Visibility and Camera, and you can define custom channels for gameplay interactions. Each UPrimitiveComponent has an object type and a response table that controls how it reacts to different trace channels — block, overlap, or ignore. Practically, you might set walls and world geometry to block Visibility while pickups block a custom interaction channel. This filtering lets you avoid irrelevant hits and improves performance by reducing post-filtering in code. A common mistake is using Visibility for everything; that can lead to unintended hits or missed hits depending on how assets were set up. Another nuance is that traces may return actors that overlap rather than block if you use the wrong channel or QueryParams; be explicit about the channel you pass to LineTraceSingleByChannel. To test your setup, place several actors with differing object types and use a trace that targets only the channel you expect. If you still get unexpected results, inspect each component’s collision preset in the editor — responses determine the outcome. In short, choose channels and set component responses so traces are precise and cheap.

keyIdea.text: Collision channels and object responses let you control what traces can hit; configure component presets and custom channels for precision.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Collision Channels
Channels & Presets
Use built-in channels like Visibility for camera and line-of-sight queries, and define custom channels for interaction and projectiles. Set each component’s object type and response to determine whether it blocks or ignores a trace channel.
ECC_Visibility
ECC_Camera
Custom: ECC_GameTraceChannel1
Practical Check
  • Set pickups to block your interaction channel only so they’re found by interaction traces.
  • Keep world geometry blocking Visibility for line-of-sight tests.
  • Use editor collision presets to verify responses per component.
Key Takeaway

Map channels to gameplay intent and use component responses to ensure traces return only relevant actors.

screens.title: FCollisionQueryParams and Trace Options
screens.narratorSegment: FCollisionQueryParams customizes how the engine performs a trace. A common need is ignoring the actor that initiated the trace so the trace doesn’t immediately hit the owner; use AddIgnoredActor for that. Another important option is bTraceComplex, which toggles between simple collision and per-polygon collision. Use complex collision when you require high accuracy, such as limb-level hit detection on a skeletal mesh, but remember it is more expensive. There are additional flags such as bReturnPhysicalMaterial when you need the physical material information for effects, or settings to ignore specific components. A typical safe setup for an interaction trace is: add the owner actor to ignored actors, set bTraceComplex to false for fast checks, and avoid returning physical material unless required. Beginners often overuse complex collision because they expect it to be universally better; in practice, choose the simplest collision that meets your gameplay need. Also, if you plan to reuse a single FCollisionQueryParams instance across many traces, ensure it’s configured appropriately each time to avoid stale ignores or flags. The practical rule is: ignore the owner, choose collision complexity deliberately, and add returns only for values you will actually use.

keyIdea.title: Query Params
keyIdea.text: Use FCollisionQueryParams to ignore actors, choose complex vs simple collision, and request additional return data when needed.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › FCollisionQueryParams
Common Settings
  • AddIgnoredActor(this) — prevent self-hits.
  • bTraceComplex — true for per-polygon accuracy, false for simple collision.
  • bReturnPhysicalMaterial — request material info only when needed.
Example Pattern
For highlighting an actor while looking: ignore the owner, use simple collision for speed, and avoid extra returns to keep traces lightweight. Switch to complex only when you need exact bone hits.
Common mistake
Forgetting to call AddIgnoredActor(this) causes the trace to hit your own capsule or camera immediately, producing false positives.

screens.title: Shape Traces: Sphere, Box, Capsule
screens.narratorSegment: Shape traces sweep a geometric volume along a path to detect anything intersecting that swept volume. SphereTrace, BoxTrace, and CapsuleTrace are common choices. Use shape traces for area-based interactions like melee sweeps, explosion radii, or when you need to cover a cone or arc without issuing many line traces. The A P I mirrors line trace usage: supply start and end points, shape dimensions such as radius or half-extents, query params, and a collision channel. The Multi variants return all hits along the sweep which is useful when multiple actors must be affected. For a melee attack, a SphereTraceMultiByChannel swept across the swing arc is typically more efficient and simpler than firing many line traces in a fan. A concrete example from the lesson is replacing repeated line traces in a fan with a single sphere sweep that returns every actor inside the swept volume. Remember to check each returned FHitResult for validity. A misconception is that shape traces are always more expensive; in many cases a single sweep is far cheaper than many discrete line traces. Choose the trace form that matches the geometry of the gameplay interaction.

keyIdea.text: Sweep a sphere, box, or capsule to detect actors across a volume; prefer multi sweeps for area effects instead of many line traces.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Shape Traces
When to use
Use shape traces for area effects, melee arcs, and any case where a volume sweep better represents the gameplay than a single line.
SphereTrace
BoxTrace
CapsuleTrace
Concrete Example
Replace many line traces in a melee swing with a single SphereTraceMultiByChannel sweeping the arc. The sweep returns all actors inside the volume, simplifying logic and improving performance.
Key Takeaway
Match trace shape to gameplay geometry: volume sweeps for area effects, line traces for precise hits.

screens.title: Implement UpdateInteractionTrace
screens.narratorSegment: Implementing UpdateInteractionTrace is a common hands-on task. The flow is: compute start and end from the camera, set up FCollisionQueryParams ignoring the player, perform a LineTraceSingleByChannel against Visibility or a custom channel, and interpret the result. If the trace hits an actor and it differs from CurrentHighlightedActor, un-highlight the previous actor and highlight the new one by enabling custom depth on its root component and setting a stencil value. If the trace hits nothing and CurrentHighlightedActor is not null, un-highlight and clear the pointer. A concrete example included in the chapter sets the trace distance to 500 units, uses simple collision for highlighting, and toggles SetRenderCustomDepth on the root primitive. A common pitfall is attempting to call SetRenderCustomDepth on an actor whose root component is not a primitive; always cast to UPrimitiveComponent before calling. Also, perform these highlights only when the highlighted actor actually changed to avoid repeated state churn. During testing, place several static meshes with collision blocking the chosen channel and walk the view to ensure highlight toggling behaves correctly. This flow keeps visuals responsive while avoiding unnecessary work each frame.

keyIdea.title: Highlight Flow
keyIdea.text: Trace each tick or on demand, compare hit actor to current highlight, toggle custom depth safely, and clear when no hit.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › UpdateInteractionTrace
Step-by-step
1. Compute Start = camera location, End = Start + forward * distance.
2. Prepare FCollisionQueryParams, AddIgnoredActor(this), set bTraceComplex appropriately.
3. Call LineTraceSingleByChannel and check boolean result.
4. If hit actor != CurrentHighlightedActor, un-highlight old and highlight new via UPrimitiveComponent SetRenderCustomDepth.
Concrete Code Tips
  • Cast GetRootComponent() to UPrimitiveComponent before toggling custom depth.
  • Only update materials or depth when the highlighted actor changes to reduce per-frame work.
  • Choose a sensible trace range, e.g., 500 units for interaction reach.
Common Pitfall
Attempting SetRenderCustomDepth on a non-primitive component will fail; always validate the cast first.

screens.title: Visualizing Traces with DrawDebug Helpers
screens.narratorSegment: Debug visualization is invaluable when traces behave unexpectedly. Unreal’s DrawDebugLine, DrawDebugSphere, and similar helpers let you see exactly what you cast. In a line trace example, draw a green line when the trace hits and red when it misses, and set a short lifetime so visuals are temporary. For shape traces, draw the initial and final shapes or the swept path to confirm radius and sweep direction. Use debug draws only in development builds because they can clutter the scene and add overhead. A practical example: after calling LineTraceSingleByChannel, draw a line from Start to End colored by bHit so you can visually verify the range and orientation. If you expected the trace to hit an actor but it misses, check the component collision presets and the channel you used. Another useful trick is to log HitResult. Location and HitResult. GetActor()->GetName() to cross-check visual results with data. A common misconception is blaming code when the trace actually uses the wrong channel; visualize the path first, then inspect component responses. In short, draw what you ask the engine to trace and you will quickly find configuration errors.

In a line trace example, draw a green line when the trace hits and red when it misses, and set a short lifetime so visuals are temporary. For shape traces, draw the initial and final shapes or the swept path to confirm radius and sweep direction. Use debug draws only in development builds because they can clutter the scene and add overhead. A practical example: after calling LineTraceSingleByChannel, draw a line from Start to End colored by bHit so you can visually verify the range and orientation. If you expected the trace to hit an actor but it misses, check the component collision presets and the channel you used. Another useful trick is to log HitResult. Location and HitResult. GetActor()->GetName() to cross-check visual results with data. screens.title: Performance Considerations
screens.narratorSegment: Tracing can be inexpensive when used sparingly, but costs grow when you run many complex traces frequently. The two main cost drivers are frequency and complexity. Running a trace every frame across many actors or using bTraceComplex true without need increases C P U work. To mitigate costs, first ask whether the trace must run every frame. For interaction traces consider running them on input or at a lower tick rate, such as ten times per second. Second, prefer simple collision unless you need per-triangle precision for accurate hits. Third, use shape sweeps to replace many line traces; a single SphereTraceMultiByChannel can be cheaper than dozens of line traces fanned across an arc. Fourth, avoid unnecessary per-hit work: only change render state when the highlighted actor actually changes. Lastly, profile your game with engine profiling tools and look for hotspots. A common misconception is that shape traces always cost more — the sweep may actually be the optimal single call for area checks. The practical rule is to measure, choose the simplest collision that works, reduce frequency, and batch where possible.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and How to Avoid Them
screens.narratorSegment: This lesson highlights frequent beginner errors and how to prevent them. First, forgetting to ignore the owner leads to traces that immediately report the actor performing the trace; always call AddIgnoredActor(this). Second, using bTraceComplex true by default may give accurate results but at a cost; choose complex collision only when you need per-polygon detail such as bone-level hits. Third, using the wrong collision channel can return unrelated objects; verify component collision presets and choose a channel aligned with gameplay intent. Fourth, attempting to toggle render custom depth without confirming the root is a primitive component can silently fail or crash when misused; cast to UPrimitiveComponent first. Fifth, updating highlight state every frame even when the actor hasn’t changed wastes C P U and render calls; only toggle state on change. To avoid these problems, follow a checklist: ignore owner, pick collision complexity intentionally, choose proper channel, cast components safely, and minimize repeated state updates. When testing, use debug visuals and logs to confirm the exact actors and hit locations returned by traces. screens.title: Hands-on: Highlight Actor When Looked At
screens.narratorSegment: Follow a concrete activity to practice tracing: implement a simple highlighted look-at system in your player character class. Add a member AActor* CurrentHighlightedActor initialized to nullptr. In Tick, call UpdateInteractionTrace. The trace should use a reasonable range like 500 units, ignore the player, and use simple collision for responsiveness. When the trace hits an actor different from CurrentHighlightedActor, un-highlight the previous actor by setting its primitive component’s custom depth off, then enable custom depth on the new actor and set a distinct stencil value. If the trace hits nothing and CurrentHighlightedActor is set, clear the highlight and set the pointer to null. A common test failure is leaving an actor highlighted after it is no longer visible; ensure your no-hit branch clears the old highlight. fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we will learn how tracing, or raycasting, connects your C++ code to the game world. Tracing simulates an invisible probe — either a single line or a swept shape — to ask what lies along a path. You will see how Unreal’s tracing functions return an FHitResult with details like the hit actor, hit location and surface normal. We will also cover configuring collision channels and FCollisionQueryParams so traces hit only what matters. Practical examples include interaction traces from a player camera to highlight objects, aiming traces for hitscan weapons, and shape traces for melee sweeps or explosion radii. Along the way we will practice safe checks so your code doesn’t assume a hit exists, and we’ll use debug drawing to visualize traces while developing. By the end of the chapter you will be able to write line and shape traces in C++, interpret FHitResult fields reliably, and choose trace settings that balance accuracy and performance. Think about one interaction in your game that depends on seeing what the player is looking at — that is where tracing matters most.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to name and implement the primary tracing methods used in Unreal Engine C++ and explain when to use each. You will read and interpret FHitResult fields to extract meaningful data like the hit actor, location, and surface normal, and you will avoid null access by checking the hit flags. You will also configure collision channels and object types to filter traces so they return only relevant actors, which improves correctness and performance. Finally, you will implement a practical interaction trace that highlights objects the player looks at using custom depth, and you will use debug drawing to inspect traces during development. Each objective includes a competency milestone so you know when you have achieved it. Expect to practice both single line traces and shape traces, and to reflect on common mistakes such as forgetting to ignore the actor performing the trace or using per-polygon collision without need. These skills cover both correctness and efficiency, which matter in every interactive game.

This second objectives slide focuses on practical outcomes and safety checks. You will implement an UpdateInteractionTrace function that runs on tick or on demand, casts a visibility trace from the player camera, and highlights the actor under the crosshair using custom depth. You will manage CurrentHighlightedActor and safely un-highlight when the trace no longer hits the actor. You will also use DrawDebug helpers during development so you can visibly confirm trace direction, hit status, and shape sweeps. Finally, you will learn two assessment ideas: choosing the right trace for a precise limb hit and using a shape trace for area sweeps. Each assessment reinforces how query parameters and collision channels affect results, and how using complex collision influences accuracy and performance. Mastering these duties gives you a repeatable pattern to add interactions to most gameplay features without causing crashes or expensive per-frame costs.

Tracing, also called raycasting, is the act of sending an invisible probe into the game world to check what it intersects. At its simplest, a line trace defines a start point and an end point; the engine walks that straight path and reports any collisions. In Unreal Engine C++ this returns an FHitResult containing the actor and component hit, the hit location, the surface normal, and other details like bone name for skeletal meshes. Think of a flashlight beam: where the beam meets an object you can learn what that object is and how to respond. A common gameplay example is pointing at a pickup item — a trace from the camera detects the item so you can show a UI prompt or pick it up. A misconception to avoid is assuming the trace always hits something. You must check the hit flag before reading fields, otherwise you risk null access. Another misconception is that traces are always cheap; they can become expensive if you run complex multi-shape traces every frame across many actors. The core takeaway is that tracing is a precise way to query the world, but you must control what you query and how often. How might you use tracing to determine whether an NPC is visible from the player’s vantage?

Let's walk through a basic line trace pattern you will use frequently. The necessary inputs are a start location, an end location — usually start plus a forward vector times distance — and a collision channel to query, such as Visibility. In C++, you prepare an FHitResult and an FCollisionQueryParams object. Important query settings include adding the actor performing the trace to the ignore list and setting bTraceComplex if you need per-polygon accuracy. Call LineTraceSingleByChannel on UWorld and check its boolean return. If true, read HitResult. GetActor(), HitResult. Location, and HitResult. Normal. A concrete example is tracing 200 or 500 units forward from the camera to detect interactable props. A common mistake is forgetting to ignore the owner; the trace may immediately hit the performing actor and return itself. Another nuance is the difference between simple collision and complex collision: simple is faster and usually sufficient for gameplay highlighting, while complex enables bone-level accuracy when you need exact hit points on a skeletal mesh. As a quick check, draw a debug line colored green on hit and red on miss so you can see the behavior while testing. How will you decide trace distance in your project?

FHitResult is the structured response you get after a trace and is central to deciding how to react. The most used fields are GetActor or HitActor, which tells you the actor hit; HitComponent gives the specific primitive component; Location is the world position of the impact; Normal describes the surface orientation at the hit point; and BoneName is available when hitting a skeletal mesh. A practical example: when detecting a headshot you rely on BoneName to confirm the limb hit, but only after you used complex collision to get per-polygon detail. Another vital aspect is the hit validity flags. Use bBlockingHit or IsValidBlockingHit to guard access. Beginners often try to cast the actor right away and crash because the trace returned no hit. Also beware that Location and Normal are only meaningful when a hit occurred; they may be zero or undefined otherwise. As a check during development, log or display the values you read from FHitResult to ensure they match expected geometry. The core takeaway is: read FHitResult carefully, guard access, and use the right collision complexity to get the fields you need.

Collision channels and object types determine what a trace actually hits. Unreal provides built-in channels like Visibility and Camera, and you can define custom channels for gameplay interactions. Each UPrimitiveComponent has an object type and a response table that controls how it reacts to different trace channels — block, overlap, or ignore. Practically, you might set walls and world geometry to block Visibility while pickups block a custom interaction channel. This filtering lets you avoid irrelevant hits and improves performance by reducing post-filtering in code. A common mistake is using Visibility for everything; that can lead to unintended hits or missed hits depending on how assets were set up. Another nuance is that traces may return actors that overlap rather than block if you use the wrong channel or QueryParams; be explicit about the channel you pass to LineTraceSingleByChannel. To test your setup, place several actors with differing object types and use a trace that targets only the channel you expect. If you still get unexpected results, inspect each component’s collision preset in the editor — responses determine the outcome. In short, choose channels and set component responses so traces are precise and cheap.

FCollisionQueryParams customizes how the engine performs a trace. A common need is ignoring the actor that initiated the trace so the trace doesn’t immediately hit the owner; use AddIgnoredActor for that. Another important option is bTraceComplex, which toggles between simple collision and per-polygon collision. Use complex collision when you require high accuracy, such as limb-level hit detection on a skeletal mesh, but remember it is more expensive. There are additional flags such as bReturnPhysicalMaterial when you need the physical material information for effects, or settings to ignore specific components. A typical safe setup for an interaction trace is: add the owner actor to ignored actors, set bTraceComplex to false for fast checks, and avoid returning physical material unless required. Beginners often overuse complex collision because they expect it to be universally better; in practice, choose the simplest collision that meets your gameplay need. Also, if you plan to reuse a single FCollisionQueryParams instance across many traces, ensure it’s configured appropriately each time to avoid stale ignores or flags. The practical rule is: ignore the owner, choose collision complexity deliberately, and add returns only for values you will actually use.

Shape traces sweep a geometric volume along a path to detect anything intersecting that swept volume. SphereTrace, BoxTrace, and CapsuleTrace are common choices. Use shape traces for area-based interactions like melee sweeps, explosion radii, or when you need to cover a cone or arc without issuing many line traces. The A P I mirrors line trace usage: supply start and end points, shape dimensions such as radius or half-extents, query params, and a collision channel. The Multi variants return all hits along the sweep which is useful when multiple actors must be affected. For a melee attack, a SphereTraceMultiByChannel swept across the swing arc is typically more efficient and simpler than firing many line traces in a fan. A concrete example from the lesson is replacing repeated line traces in a fan with a single sphere sweep that returns every actor inside the swept volume. Remember to check each returned FHitResult for validity. A misconception is that shape traces are always more expensive; in many cases a single sweep is far cheaper than many discrete line traces. Choose the trace form that matches the geometry of the gameplay interaction.

Implementing UpdateInteractionTrace is a common hands-on task. The flow is: compute start and end from the camera, set up FCollisionQueryParams ignoring the player, perform a LineTraceSingleByChannel against Visibility or a custom channel, and interpret the result. If the trace hits an actor and it differs from CurrentHighlightedActor, un-highlight the previous actor and highlight the new one by enabling custom depth on its root component and setting a stencil value. If the trace hits nothing and CurrentHighlightedActor is not null, un-highlight and clear the pointer. A concrete example included in the chapter sets the trace distance to 500 units, uses simple collision for highlighting, and toggles SetRenderCustomDepth on the root primitive. A common pitfall is attempting to call SetRenderCustomDepth on an actor whose root component is not a primitive; always cast to UPrimitiveComponent before calling. Also, perform these highlights only when the highlighted actor actually changed to avoid repeated state churn. During testing, place several static meshes with collision blocking the chosen channel and walk the view to ensure highlight toggling behaves correctly. This flow keeps visuals responsive while avoiding unnecessary work each frame.

Debug visualization is invaluable when traces behave unexpectedly. Unreal’s DrawDebugLine, DrawDebugSphere, and similar helpers let you see exactly what you cast. In a line trace example, draw a green line when the trace hits and red when it misses, and set a short lifetime so visuals are temporary. If you expected the trace to hit an actor but it misses, check the component collision presets and the channel you used. Another useful trick is to log HitResult. Location and HitResult. GetActor()->GetName() to cross-check visual results with data. A common misconception is blaming code when the trace actually uses the wrong channel; visualize the path first, then inspect component responses. In short, draw what you ask the engine to trace and you will quickly find configuration errors.

Running a trace every frame across many actors or using bTraceComplex true without need increases C P U work. To mitigate costs, first ask whether the trace must run every frame. Fourth, avoid unnecessary per-hit work: only change render state when the highlighted actor actually changes. Lastly, profile your game with engine profiling tools and look for hotspots. A common misconception is that shape traces always cost more — the sweep may actually be the optimal single call for area checks. The practical rule is to measure, choose the simplest collision that works, reduce frequency, and batch where possible.
